claim: Precursor ribosomal RNA (pre-rRNA) processing is a key step in ribosome biosynthesis and involves numerous RNases.
source: Precursor ribosomal RNA (pre-rRNA) processing is a key step in ribosome biosynthesis and involves numerous RNases.
evidence: This is a general statement about pre-rRNA processing that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field of ribosome biosynthesis.

claim: A HEPN (higher eukaryote and prokaryote nucleotide binding) nuclease Las1 and a polynucleotide kinase Grc3 assemble into a tetramerase responsible for rRNA maturation.
source: A HEPN (higher eukaryote and prokaryote nucleotide binding) nuclease Las1 and a polynucleotide kinase Grc3 assemble into a tetramerase responsible for rRNA maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript showing the tetrameric assembly.

claim: The structures of full-length Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Cyberlindnera jadinii Las1-Grc3 complexes were determined.
source: Here, we report the structures of full-length Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Cyberlindnera jadinii Las1-Grc3 complexes, and C. jadinii Las1.
evidence: The manuscript presents crystallographic and cryo-EM data for these structures.

claim: The structure of C. jadinii Las1 was determined.
source: Here, we report the structures of full-length Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Cyberlindnera jadinii Las1-Grc3 complexes, and C. jadinii Las1.
evidence: The manuscript presents crystallographic data for the CjLas1 HEPN domain structure.

claim: The central coiled-coil domain of Las1 facilitates pre-rRNA binding and cleavage.
source: The Las1-Grc3 structures show that the central coiled-coil domain of Las1 facilitates pre-rRNA binding and cleavage, while the Grc3 C-terminal loop motif directly binds to the HEPN active center of Las1 and regulates pre-rRNA cleavage.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays showing that the CC domain contributes to ITS2 RNA binding and facilitates cleavage.

claim: The Grc3 C-terminal loop motif directly binds to the HEPN active center of Las1 and regulates pre-rRNA cleavage.
source: The Las1-Grc3 structures show that the central coiled-coil domain of Las1 facilitates pre-rRNA binding and cleavage, while the Grc3 C-terminal loop motif directly binds to the HEPN active center of Las1 and regulates pre-rRNA cleavage.
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing the GCT binding to the HEPN active center and mutagenesis data showing loss of activity upon mutation.

claim: Grc3 binding induces conformational rearrangements of catalytic residues associated with HEPN nuclease activation.
source: Structural comparison between Las1 and Las1-Grc3 complex exhibits that Grc3 binding induces conformational rearrangements of catalytic residues associated with HEPN nuclease activation.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison showing conformational changes in the catalytic pocket upon Grc3 binding.

claim: Las1 processes pre-rRNA at two specific sites (C2 and C2′).
source: Biochemical assays identify that Las1 processes pre-rRNA at the two specific sites (C2 and C2′), which greatly facilitates rRNA maturation.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assays and RNA sequencing data identifying the two cleavage sites.

claim: Las1 processing at C2 and C2′ sites greatly facilitates rRNA maturation.
source: Biochemical assays identify that Las1 processes pre-rRNA at the two specific sites (C2 and C2′), which greatly facilitates rRNA maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequential cleavage pattern and the role of these cleavages in the rRNA maturation pathway.

claim: Ribosomes are large molecular machines assembled from numerous proteins and RNAs that are responsible for protein synthesis in cells.
source: Ribosomes are large molecular machines assembled from numerous proteins and RNAs that are responsible for protein synthesis in cells (Anger et al., 2013; Gasse et al., 2015; Khatter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In eukaryotes, ribosome biosynthesis is tightly coupled to cell growth and cell cycle progression.
source: In eukaryotes, ribosome biosynthesis is tightly coupled to cell growth and cell cycle progression and is critical for regulating normal cell size and maintaining cell cycle progression (Castle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ribosome biosynthesis is critical for regulating normal cell size and maintaining cell cycle progression.
source: In eukaryotes, ribosome biosynthesis is tightly coupled to cell growth and cell cycle progression and is critical for regulating normal cell size and maintaining cell cycle progression (Castle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ribosome biosynthesis is an extremely complicated process involving about 200 assembly and processing factors.
source: Ribosome biosynthesis is an extremely complicated process involving about 200 assembly and processing factors, which are involved in a series of continuous assembly and processing reactions such as ribosome protein folding, modification, assembly, and precursor rRNA (pre-rRNA) processing (Gasse et al., 2015; Lafontaine, 2015; Pillon et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mature ribosomes in yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae contain 79 proteins and four RNAs (25S, 18S, 5.8S, and 5S rRNA).
source: Mature ribosomes in yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae contain 79 proteins and four RNAs (25S, 18S, 5.8S, and 5S rRNA) (Doudna and Rath, 2002; Wilson and Doudna Cate, 2012; Woolford and Baserga, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 5S rRNA is transcribed by RNA polymerase III.
source: 5S rRNA is transcribed by RNA polymerase III, whereas 25S, 18S, and 5.8S rRNA are cotranscribed by RNA polymerase I as a single long precursor (35S pre-rRNA) (Tomecki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: 25S, 18S, and 5.8S rRNA are cotranscribed by RNA polymerase I as a single long precursor (35S pre-rRNA).
source: 5S rRNA is transcribed by RNA polymerase III, whereas 25S, 18S, and 5.8S rRNA are cotranscribed by RNA polymerase I as a single long precursor (35S pre-rRNA) (Tomecki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The 35S pre-rRNA includes 5′-external transcribed spacer sequence (ETS), 3′-external transcribed spacer sequence, and two internal transcribed spacer sequences (ITS1 and ITS2).
source: Except 25S, 18S, and 5.8S rRNA sequences, the 35S pre-rRNA also includes 5′-external transcribed spacer sequence (ETS), 3′-external transcribed spacer sequence, and two internal transcribed spacer sequences (ITS1 and ITS2) (Fromm et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: ITS1 is located between 5.8S and 18S rRNA.
source: ITS1 is located between 5.8S and 18S rRNA, and ITS2 is located between 5.8S and 25S rRNA (Coleman, 2003; Côté et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ITS2 is located between 5.8S and 25S rRNA.
source: ITS1 is located between 5.8S and 18S rRNA, and ITS2 is located between 5.8S and 25S rRNA (Coleman, 2003; Côté et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mature rRNAs are generated by a large number of endonucleases and exonucleases that remove transcribed spacers step by step through multiple efficient and correct processing reactions.
source: The mature rRNAs are generated by a large number of endonucleases and exonucleases that remove these transcribed spacers step by step through multiple efficient and correct processing reactions (Granneman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Pre-rRNA processing factors synergistically produce mature rRNAs and lead to accurate and efficient assembly of mature ribosome in the nucleolus.
source: The pre-rRNA processing factors synergistically produce mature rRNAs and lead to an accurate and efficient assembly of mature ribosome in the nucleolus, which are key to cell survival (Pillon and Stanley, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Accurate and efficient ribosome assembly is key to cell survival.
source: The pre-rRNA processing factors synergistically produce mature rRNAs and lead to an accurate and efficient assembly of mature ribosome in the nucleolus, which are key to cell survival (Pillon and Stanley, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mutations in the genes that encode pre-rRNA processing factors are often lethal.
source: Mutations in the genes that encode these pre-rRNA processing factors are often lethal (Tomecki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Las1 and Grc3 are highly conserved proteins.
source: Las1 and Grc3 are highly conserved proteins and have recently been identified as core enzymes involved in processing and removing ITS2 spacer, which is a key step in the synthesis of 60S ribosomal subunit (Gasse et al., 2015; Schillewaert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Las1 and Grc3 are core enzymes involved in processing and removing ITS2 spacer.
source: Las1 and Grc3 are highly conserved proteins and have recently been identified as core enzymes involved in processing and removing ITS2 spacer, which is a key step in the synthesis of 60S ribosomal subunit (Gasse et al., 2015; Schillewaert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Processing and removing ITS2 spacer is a key step in the synthesis of 60S ribosomal subunit.
source: Las1 and Grc3 are highly conserved proteins and have recently been identified as core enzymes involved in processing and removing ITS2 spacer, which is a key step in the synthesis of 60S ribosomal subunit (Gasse et al., 2015; Schillewaert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Las1 is a nucleolar protein essential for ribosome biogenesis.
source: Las1 is characterized as a nucleolar protein essential for ribosome biogenesis, as well as cell proliferation and cell viability in S. cerevisiae (Castle et al., 2012; Castle et al., 2010; Doseff and Arndt, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Las1 is essential for cell proliferation and cell viability in S. cerevisiae.
source: Las1 is characterized as a nucleolar protein essential for ribosome biogenesis, as well as cell proliferation and cell viability in S. cerevisiae (Castle et al., 2012; Castle et al., 2010; Doseff and Arndt, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Las1 is an endoribonuclease that contains a HEPN domain responsible for rRNA processing.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that Las1 is an endoribonuclease that contains a HEPN (higher eukaryote and prokaryote nucleotide binding) domain responsible for rRNA processing (Pillon et al., 2020; Pillon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The HEPN domain must be dimerized to form an active nuclease.
source: The HEPN domain must be dimerized to form an active nuclease, such as the Cas13 effectors in CRISPR immune defense systems, whose catalytic site is formed by two HEPN domains involved in non-specific cleavage of single-stranded RNA (Knott et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017a ; Liu et al., 2017b ; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cas13 effectors in CRISPR immune defense systems have a catalytic site formed by two HEPN domains involved in non-specific cleavage of single-stranded RNA.
source: The HEPN domain must be dimerized to form an active nuclease, such as the Cas13 effectors in CRISPR immune defense systems, whose catalytic site is formed by two HEPN domains involved in non-specific cleavage of single-stranded RNA (Knott et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017a ; Liu et al., 2017b ; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Las1 specifically cleaves at the C2 site within ITS2 and generates the 7S pre-rRNA and 26S pre-rRNA.
source: Interestingly, Las1 specifically cleaves at the C2 site within ITS2 and generates the 7S pre-rRNA and 26S pre-rRNA ( Fernández-Pevida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The cleavage activity of Las1 is primarily dependent on Grc3.
source: In addition, the cleavage activity of Las1 is primarily dependent on another enzyme Grc3.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays showing that Las1 has weak activity without Grc3 but robust activity in the presence of Grc3.

claim: Grc3 is a polynucleotide kinase responsible for Las1 nuclease activation.
source: Grc3 is a polynucleotide kinase responsible not only for Las1 nuclease activation, but also for nonspecific phosphorylation of the 5′-OH of the 26S pre-rRNA produced by Las1 cleavage, providing a signal for further processing by Rat1-Rai1 exonuclease (Gordon et al., 2019; Xiang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Grc3 is responsible for nonspecific phosphorylation of the 5′-OH of the 26S pre-rRNA produced by Las1 cleavage.
source: Grc3 is a polynucleotide kinase responsible not only for Las1 nuclease activation, but also for nonspecific phosphorylation of the 5′-OH of the 26S pre-rRNA produced by Las1 cleavage, providing a signal for further processing by Rat1-Rai1 exonuclease (Gordon et al., 2019; Xiang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and by phosphorylation assays in the manuscript.

claim: Grc3 phosphorylation provides a signal for further processing by Rat1-Rai1 exonuclease.
source: Grc3 is a polynucleotide kinase responsible not only for Las1 nuclease activation, but also for nonspecific phosphorylation of the 5′-OH of the 26S pre-rRNA produced by Las1 cleavage, providing a signal for further processing by Rat1-Rai1 exonuclease (Gordon et al., 2019; Xiang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and by degradation assays showing Rat1-Rai1 processes phosphorylated products.

claim: Cryo-EM reveals cross-linked Chaetomium thermophilum Las1 and Grc3 assemble into a super-dimer.
source: Although cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) reveals cross-linked Chaetomium thermophilum (Ct) Las1 and Grc3 assemble into a super-dimer, due to flexibility, critical structural information is missing for the coiled-coil (CC) domain of Las1 and the N-terminal and C-terminal regions of Grc3 (Pillon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Critical structural information is missing for the coiled-coil domain of Las1 and the N-terminal and C-terminal regions of Grc3 in the Chaetomium thermophilum Las1-Grc3 structure due to flexibility.
source: Although cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) reveals cross-linked Chaetomium thermophilum (Ct) Las1 and Grc3 assemble into a super-dimer, due to flexibility, critical structural information is missing for the coiled-coil (CC) domain of Las1 and the N-terminal and C-terminal regions of Grc3 (Pillon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: S. cerevisiae Las1 endoribonuclease initially cleaves ITS2 in a step-by-step fashion at two specific sites.
source: In this study, we identified that S. cerevisiae (Sc) Las1 endoribonuclease initially cleaves ITS2 in a step-by-step fashion at two specific sites, which greatly promotes the maturation of 25S rRNA.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assays and RNA sequencing data.

claim: Las1 cleavage at two specific sites greatly promotes the maturation of 25S rRNA.
source: In this study, we identified that S. cerevisiae (Sc) Las1 endoribonuclease initially cleaves ITS2 in a step-by-step fashion at two specific sites, which greatly promotes the maturation of 25S rRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequential cleavage pattern and the role in the rRNA maturation pathway.

claim: The crystal structures of full-length ScLas1-Grc3 complex and CjLas1-Grc3 complex were solved.
source: Additionally, we solved the crystal structures of full-length ScLas1-Grc3 complex and Cyberlindnera jadinii (Cj) Las1-Grc3 complex, as well as the high-resolution structure of CjLas1 HEPN domain.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The high-resolution structure of CjLas1 HEPN domain was solved.
source: Additionally, we solved the crystal structures of full-length ScLas1-Grc3 complex and Cyberlindnera jadinii (Cj) Las1-Grc3 complex, as well as the high-resolution structure of CjLas1 HEPN domain.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HEPN endoribonucleases such as Cas13, Ire1, and RNase L are metal-independent RNA-specific enzymes that efficiently cleave substrate RNA at multiple sites.
source: HEPN endoribonucleases such as Cas13, Ire1, and RNase L are metal-independent RNA-specific enzymes that efficiently cleave substrate RNA at multiple sites (Abudayyeh et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2014; Korennykh et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Las1 is a HEPN-containing RNase.
source: Las1 is also identified as a HEPN-containing RNase, but it has only been found to initially cut ITS2 RNA at a single specific position (C2).
evidence: This is supported by previous literature and the structural data in the manuscript.

claim: Las1 has only been found to initially cut ITS2 RNA at a single specific position (C2) prior to this study.
source: Las1 is also identified as a HEPN-containing RNase, but it has only been found to initially cut ITS2 RNA at a single specific position (C2).
evidence: This is based on previous literature, which is contrasted with the new findings in this manuscript.

claim: Las1 shows weak or no detectable activity to ITS2 in the absence of Grc3.
source: Las1 shows weak or no detectable activity to ITS2 in the absence of Grc3, but exhibits robust activity in the presence of Grc3 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), revealing Grc3-dependent Las1 nuclease activation.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assays shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Las1 exhibits robust activity to ITS2 in the presence of Grc3.
source: Las1 shows weak or no detectable activity to ITS2 in the absence of Grc3, but exhibits robust activity in the presence of Grc3 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), revealing Grc3-dependent Las1 nuclease activation.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro cleavage assays shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Las1 nuclease activation is Grc3-dependent.
source: Las1 shows weak or no detectable activity to ITS2 in the absence of Grc3, but exhibits robust activity in the presence of Grc3 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), revealing Grc3-dependent Las1 nuclease activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Las1 activity with and without Grc3.

claim: A single 5′-Cy5-labeled cleavage product was observed in the ITS2 cleavage assay.
source: Interestingly, we observed a single 5′-Cy5-labeled cleavage product, and two prominent 3′-Cy3-labeled cleavage products including a final product and an intermediate product (Figure 1B), suggesting that cleavage of ITS2 substrate occurs at two specific sites.
evidence: This is supported by the cleavage assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Two prominent 3′-Cy3-labeled cleavage products including a final product and an intermediate product were observed in the ITS2 cleavage assay.
source: Interestingly, we observed a single 5′-Cy5-labeled cleavage product, and two prominent 3′-Cy3-labeled cleavage products including a final product and an intermediate product (Figure 1B), suggesting that cleavage of ITS2 substrate occurs at two specific sites.

claim: Cleavage of ITS2 substrate occurs at two specific sites.
source: Interestingly, we observed a single 5′-Cy5-labeled cleavage product, and two prominent 3′-Cy3-labeled cleavage products including a final product and an intermediate product (Figure 1B), suggesting that cleavage of ITS2 substrate occurs at two specific sites.

claim: The 33-nt ITS2 substrate RNA harbors the C2 site, which is located between nucleotides A140 and G141.
source: The 33-nt ITS2 substrate RNA harbors the C2 site, which is located between nucleotides A140 and G141 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on the RNA sequence shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ScLas1 cleaves the 33-nt ITS2 at the C2 site to theoretically generate a 10-nt 5′-terminal product and a 23-nt 3′-terminal product.
source: ScLas1 cleaves the 33-nt ITS2 at the C2 site to theoretically generate a 10-nt 5′-terminal product and a 23-nt 3′-terminal product (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on the RNA sequence and the known C2 cleavage site.

claim: The 23-nt 3′-terminal product is an intermediate that can be further processed by Las1 at a specific site to produce two small products.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that the 23-nt 3′-terminal product is an intermediate that can be further processed by Las1 at a specific site to produce two small products.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of multiple cleavage products.

claim: Four cleavage bands were observed in the unlabeled 33-nt ITS2 RNA cleavage assay: two approximately 23-nt (P2) and 14-nt (P3) in length, and two (P1 and P4) less than 11-nt in length.
source: We observed four cleavage bands, two approximately 23-nt (P2) and 14-nt (P3) in length, and two (P1 and P4) less than 11-nt in length (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the cleavage assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The 23-nt product (P2) is an intermediate cleavage product, which is further cleaved to generate 14-nt and 9-nt products.
source: The 23-nt product (P2) is obviously an intermediate cleavage product, which is further cleaved to generate 14-nt and 9-nt products.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of multiple cleavage products and their sizes.

claim: The C2′ cleavage site is located between nucleotides G154 and C155.
source: Based on these observations, we identify that another cleavage site, which we designated as C2′, is located between nucleotides G154 and C155.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Las1 is able to process ITS2 at the C2 and C2′ sites in a step-by-step manner, resulting in a 9-nt 3′-end product and a 10-nt 5′-end product.
source: Las1 is able to process ITS2 at the C2 and C2′ sites in a step-by-step manner, resulting in a 9-nt 3′-end product and a 10-nt 5′-end product.
evidence: This is supported by the cleavage assay data and RNA sequencing data.

claim: The C2 site is located between nucleotides A140 and G141.
source: We used an adaptor RNA to separately link the product RNA fragments to form template RNAs. After reverse transcription and sequencing of these template RNAs, we obtained the accurate sequence information for products P2 and P4, revealing that the C2 site is located between nucleotides A140 and G141, and the C2′ site is located between nucleotides G154 and C155.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The cleavage products P2, P3, and P4 are all phosphorylated by Grc3 in the presence of ATP.
source: The cleavage products P2, P3, and P4 are all phosphorylated by Grc3 as they all show a slight shift when in the presence of ATP in the reaction (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Las1 generates 5′-OH terminus following both C2 and C2′ cleavage.
source: This indicates that Las1 generates 5′-OH terminus following both C2 and C2′ cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cleavage products are phosphorylated by Grc3.

claim: The phosphorylated products are further degraded by Rat1-Rai1 exonuclease.
source: The phosphorylated products are further degraded by Rat1-Rai1 exonuclease, especially P2 and P4, which are completely degraded under given experimental conditions (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by the degradation assay data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: P2 and P4 are completely degraded by Rat1-Rai1 exonuclease under given experimental conditions.
source: The phosphorylated products are further degraded by Rat1-Rai1 exonuclease, especially P2 and P4, which are completely degraded under given experimental conditions (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by the degradation assay data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: P3 is likely too short to degrade completely by Rat1-Rai1 exonuclease.
source: P3 is likely too short to degrade completely.

claim: Mutations in the HEPN catalytic residues of Las1 abolish C2 and C2′ cleavage.

evidence: This is supported by the mutagenesis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both C2 and C2′ cleavages are attributed to metal-independent Las1 RNase.

evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data and the metal independence assay.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of ScLas1-Grc3 complex was determined at 3.07 Å resolution.
source: To elucidate how Las1 and Grc3 cooperate to direct ITS2 cleavage and phosphorylation, we determined the cryo-EM and crystal structures of full-length ScLas1-Grc3 complex at 3.07 Å and 3.69 Å resolution (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Tables 1 and 2), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data presented in Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The crystal structure of ScLas1-Grc3 complex was determined at 3.69 Å resolution.
source: To elucidate how Las1 and Grc3 cooperate to direct ITS2 cleavage and phosphorylation, we determined the cryo-EM and crystal structures of full-length ScLas1-Grc3 complex at 3.07 Å and 3.69 Å resolution (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Tables 1 and 2), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: ScGrc3 can activate ScLas1 nuclease well for ITS2 cleavage.
source: Cleavage assay indicates that ScGrc3 can activate ScLas1 nuclease well for ITS2 cleavage, while CjGrc3 exhibits relatively weak activation ability for CjLas1 nuclease (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: CjGrc3 exhibits relatively weak activation ability for CjLas1 nuclease.
source: Cleavage assay indicates that ScGrc3 can activate ScLas1 nuclease well for ITS2 cleavage, while CjGrc3 exhibits relatively weak activation ability for CjLas1 nuclease (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cleavage assay data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of CjLas1-Grc3 complex was determined at 3.39 Å resolution.

claim: The crystal structure of CjLas1-Grc3 complex was determined at 3.39 Å resolution.
source: To better understand the differences in the mechanisms of Grc3 activation of Las1 between different species, we also solved the cryo-EM and crystal structures of full-length CjLas1-Grc3 complex at 3.39 Å and 3.39 Å resolution (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Tables 1 and 2), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: The crystal structures were solved by molecular replacement method with the cryo-EM maps of Las1-Grc3 complexes.
source: To be noted, the crystal structures were solved by molecular replacement method with the cryo-EM maps of Las1-Grc3 complexes.
evidence: This describes the method used for structure determination.

claim: The crystal structures have similar quality and resolve more structural information than the cryo-EM structures.
source: Since the crystal structures have similar quality and resolve more structural information than the cryo-EM structures (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), the subsequent presentations and descriptions are based more on the crystal structures.

claim: Las1 and Grc3 assemble into a tetramer with two copies of each.
source: Both structures reveal that Las1 and Grc3 assemble into a tetramer with two copies of each (Figures 2B and C and 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: In the tetramer, one Las1 and Grc3 molecules form a C2 symmetry with another Las1 and Grc3 molecules.
source: In the tetramer, one Las1 and Grc3 molecules form a C2 symmetry with another Las1 and Grc3 molecules.

source: Las1 consists of a relatively conserved N-terminal HEPN domain, a poorly conserved central CC domain, and a short C-terminal tail motif (LCT) (Figures 2A and 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: Grc3 is composed of an N-terminal domain (NTD), a central polynucleotide kinase (PNK) domain, a C-terminal domain (CTD), and a short C-terminal loop motif (GCT).
source: Grc3 is composed of an N-terminal domain (NTD), a central polynucleotide kinase (PNK) domain, a C-terminal domain (CTD), and a short C-terminal loop motif (GCT).

claim: A CC domain of Las1 and a copy of Grc3 are assembled into an architecture similar to one wing of a butterfly.
source: A CC domain of Las1 and a copy of Grc3 are assembled into an architecture similar to one wing of a butterfly.
evidence: This is a descriptive analogy based on the structural data.

source: The NTD and PNK domains of Grc3 constitute the forewing, while the CTD domain of Grc3 and the CC domain of Las1 form the hindwing.

claim: The CTD domain of Grc3 and the CC domain of Las1 form the hindwing of the butterfly-like architecture.
source: The NTD and PNK domains of Grc3 constitute the forewing, while the CTD domain of Grc3 and the CC domain of Las1 form the hindwing.
evidence: This is a descriptive analogy based on the structural data.

claim: All domains are perfectly stacked together to build a compact and stable tetramer architecture.
source: All domains are perfectly stacked together to build a compact and stable tetramer architecture (Figures 2C and 3C).
